questions.stem: The sentence below is divided into four parts. Identify the part containing a grammatical error: '(A) He don't / (B) know the answer / (C) to this / (D) difficult question.'
questions.explanation: Error in (A): 'don't' should be 'doesn't'. Subject-verb agreement rule: third-person singular (He/She/It) takes 'does not' (doesn't), not 'do not' (don't). Correct: 'He doesn't know the answer.'
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: The sentence below is divided into four parts. Identify the part containing a grammatical error: '(A) She bought / (B) a umbrella / (C) before the / (D) rain started.'
questions.explanation: Error in (B): 'a umbrella' should be 'an umbrella'. Use the article 'an' (not 'a') before words beginning with a vowel sound. 'Umbrella' starts with the vowel sound /ʌ/.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: The sentence below is divided into four parts. Identify the part containing a grammatical error: '(A) The teacher asked / (B) the students to / (C) open their's books / (D) and start reading.'
questions.explanation: Error in (C): 'their's' is incorrect. Possessive pronouns (my, your, his, her, its, our, their) never take an apostrophe. The correct form is simply 'their books'.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: The sentence below is divided into four parts. Identify the part containing a grammatical error: '(A) She has been / (B) working at this company / (C) for the last five years / (D) since she was graduated.'
questions.explanation: Error in (D): 'was graduated' should be 'graduated'. The verb 'graduate' is used intransitively in this context (graduate from a college). The passive form 'was graduated' is a common error. Correct: 'since she graduated'.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: The sentence below is divided into four parts. Identify the part containing a grammatical error: '(A) Between you and I, / (B) the manager made / (C) several serious errors / (D) in the report.'
questions.explanation: Error in (A): 'Between you and I' should be 'Between you and me'. Prepositions (between, with, for, etc.) must be followed by object case pronouns. 'I' is a subject pronoun; 'me' is the correct object pronoun here.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: The sentence below is divided into four parts. Identify the part containing a grammatical error: '(A) He is / (B) more taller / (C) than his elder / (D) brother.'
questions.explanation: Error in (B): 'more taller' is a double comparative. Adjectives already in comparative form (-er) do not take 'more'. Correct: 'taller' (not 'more taller'). Similarly, avoid 'more better', 'more faster', etc.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: The sentence below is divided into four parts. Identify the part containing a grammatical error: '(A) Neither the students / (B) nor the teacher / (C) were present / (D) in the classroom.'
questions.explanation: Error in (C): 'were present' should be 'was present'. With 'Neither...nor', the verb agrees with the subject nearest to it. The nearest subject is 'the teacher' (singular), so the verb must be 'was'. Correct: 'was present'.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: The sentence below is divided into four parts. Identify the part containing a grammatical error: '(A) I could not / (B) sleep properly last night / (C) because of / (D) the too much noise.'
questions.explanation: Error in (D): 'the too much noise' should be 'too much noise'. The definite article 'the' is not used with 'too much + noun'. Correct: 'because of too much noise'.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: The sentence below is divided into four parts. Identify the part containing a grammatical error: '(A) If I would have known / (B) about the exam, / (C) I would have / (D) prepared well.'
questions.explanation: Error in (A): 'If I would have known' should be 'If I had known'. In Third Conditional, the if-clause uses Past Perfect (had + V3), not 'would have'. 'Would have' belongs only in the result clause. Correct: 'If I had known about the exam, I would have prepared well.'
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: The sentence below is divided into four parts. Identify the part containing a grammatical error: '(A) She performed / (B) very good in / (C) the interview and / (D) got the job.'
questions.explanation: Error in (B): 'very good' should be 'very well'. 'Performed' is an action verb and must be modified by an adverb ('well'), not an adjective ('good'). Adjectives modify nouns; adverbs modify verbs. Correct: 'She performed very well.'
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: The sentence below is divided into four parts. Identify the part containing a grammatical error: '(A) He is / (B) one of the best / (C) player in / (D) the entire tournament.'
questions.explanation: Error in (C): 'player' should be 'players'. After 'one of the + superlative', the noun that follows must always be plural. Correct: 'He is one of the best players in the entire tournament.'
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: The sentence below is divided into four parts. Identify the part containing a grammatical error: '(A) The committee / (B) has reviewed / (C) all the proposals / (D) and submitted their report.'
questions.explanation: Error in (D): 'their report' should be 'its report'. 'Committee' is a singular collective noun and takes a singular pronoun 'its'. Treating it as plural ('their') is a common pronoun-agreement error. Correct: 'submitted its report'.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: The sentence below is divided into four parts. Identify the part containing a grammatical error: '(A) Me and my friend / (B) went to the market / (C) to buy some / (D) fresh vegetables.'
questions.explanation: Error in (A): 'Me and my friend' should be 'My friend and I'. As the subject of the verb 'went', the subject pronoun 'I' (not object pronoun 'me') is required. By convention, the speaker mentions themselves last. Correct: 'My friend and I went...'
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: The sentence below is divided into four parts. Identify the part containing a grammatical error: '(A) She is married / (B) with a doctor / (C) who works / (D) at a government hospital.'
questions.explanation: Error in (B): 'married with' should be 'married to'. The correct preposition with 'married' is 'to', not 'with'. Correct: 'She is married to a doctor.' A common error influenced by Indian English usage.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: The sentence below is divided into four parts. Identify the part containing a grammatical error: '(A) Everyone in / (B) the office / (C) have to submit / (D) their daily report.'
questions.explanation: Error in (C): 'have to submit' should be 'has to submit'. 'Everyone' is a singular indefinite pronoun and requires a singular verb. Correct: 'Everyone in the office has to submit their daily report.' Note: 'their' as a singular pronoun in (D) is now accepted.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: The sentence below is divided into four parts. Identify the part containing a grammatical error: '(A) The reason / (B) for his absence / (C) is because / (D) he was feeling unwell.'
questions.explanation: Error in (C): 'is because' should be 'is that'. 'The reason is because' is redundant since 'because' itself means 'for the reason that'. The correct structure is 'The reason...is that...'. Correct: 'The reason for his absence is that he was feeling unwell.'
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: The sentence below is divided into four parts. Identify the part containing a grammatical error: '(A) She always / (B) insists on / (C) her rights / (D) and demands it to be respected.'
options: (D) and demands it to be respected
questions.explanation: Error in (D): 'it' should be 'them'. The pronoun must agree with its antecedent 'her rights' (plural). Correct: 'and demands them to be respected.'
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: The sentence below is divided into four parts. Identify the part containing a grammatical error: '(A) Inspite of his hard work, / (B) he could not / (C) clear the examination / (D) in the first attempt.'
questions.explanation: Error in (A): 'Inspite' is a spelling error. The correct form is two words: 'In spite of'. This is a very common error in competitive exams. Correct: 'In spite of his hard work, he could not clear the examination.'
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: The sentence below is divided into four parts. Identify the part containing a grammatical error: '(A) He told me / (B) that he will meet / (C) me the / (D) following morning.'
questions.explanation: Error in (B): 'will meet' should be 'would meet'. In reported/indirect speech, the past reporting verb 'told' requires the future 'will' to shift to 'would'. Correct: 'He told me that he would meet me the following morning.'
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: The sentence below is divided into four parts. Identify the part containing a grammatical error: '(A) No sooner / (B) did the teacher enter / (C) when the students / (D) stood up to greet her.'
questions.explanation: Error in (C): 'when' should be 'than'. The fixed correlative pair is 'No sooner...than', not 'No sooner...when'. Contrast: 'Hardly/Scarcely...when/before' (correct). Correct: 'No sooner did the teacher enter than the students stood up.'
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: The sentence below is divided into four parts. Identify the part containing a grammatical error: '(A) The politicians / (B) discussed the bill / (C) and eventually all / (D) reached to a consensus.'
questions.explanation: Error in (D): 'reached to a consensus' should be 'reached a consensus'. The verb 'reach' takes a direct object without a preposition. 'Reach to' is not standard; you simply 'reach a decision/conclusion/consensus'. Correct: 'reached a consensus'.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: The sentence below is divided into four parts. Identify the part containing a grammatical error: '(A) He is too / (B) much intelligent / (C) to make such / (D) a silly mistake.'
questions.explanation: Error in (B): 'much intelligent' should be removed; the sentence should read 'He is too intelligent...'. In 'too + adjective' construction, 'much' is not inserted before the adjective. 'Too much' is used before nouns or uncountable nouns, not before adjectives.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: The sentence below is divided into four parts. Identify the part containing a grammatical error: '(A) Much people / (B) gathered outside / (C) the parliament / (D) to protest against the new law.'
options: (D) to protest against the new law
questions.explanation: Error in (A): 'Much people' should be 'Many people'. 'Much' is used with uncountable nouns (much water, much time). 'People' is a countable plural noun and requires 'many'. Correct: 'Many people gathered outside the parliament.'
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: The sentence below is divided into four parts. Identify the part containing a grammatical error: '(A) She congratulated / (B) him for / (C) winning the / (D) prestigious price.'
questions.explanation: Error in (D): 'price' should be 'prize'. These are commonly confused homophones. 'Price' means the cost of something; 'prize' means an award or honour given for winning. Correct: 'winning the prestigious prize'.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: The sentence below is divided into four parts. Identify the part containing a grammatical error: '(A) The minister along with / (B) his officials / (C) were present / (D) at the inauguration ceremony.'
questions.explanation: Error in (C): 'were present' should be 'was present'. When 'along with', 'as well as', or 'together with' connects a singular subject to additional nouns, the verb agrees with the main (singular) subject. Here, the main subject is 'The minister' (singular) → 'was present'.
questions.subject: English
